blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an m × n matrix, if any cell is `0`, set its **entire row and column** to `0`. Do it **in place**.

blocks.alt: Before: [[1,1,1],[1,0,1],[1,1,1]] with a single 0 in the middle. After: row 1 and column 1 are all zeros: [[1,0,1],[0,0,0],[1,0,1]].

blocks.text: Example
Understanding the problem
Only the zeros that were in the **original** matrix count. That sounds obvious, but it's exactly where the natural first attempt goes wrong.
The trap: zeroing as you go

Suppose you scan the matrix and, the moment you find a 0, zero its row and column. The zeros you just wrote look exactly like original zeros — so when the scan reaches them, it zeroes **their** rows and columns too, and the damage spreads until almost everything is 0.

blocks.alt: Zeroing as you scan cascades: the first 0 zeroes its row and column, then the scan finds those new zeros and keeps spreading until the whole matrix is zero.

elements.text: the new zeros trigger more zeroing…
elements.originalText: the new zeros trigger more zeroing…

blocks.text: So the work must happen in two phases: first **record** which rows and columns contain a zero, then **apply** it.
Approach 1: remember rows and columns in sets
Clear and correct: **O(m × n) time** with **O(m + n) extra space** for the two sets. The follow-up asks: can you do it with **O(1)** extra space?
The key insight: use the matrix as its own notepad

Instead of separate sets, store the markers **inside the matrix**. Use the first row as the "this column must be zeroed" list and the first column as the "this row must be zeroed" list. When `matrix[r][c]` is 0, write 0 at `matrix[r][0]` and `matrix[0][c]`.

blocks.alt: The first row and first column act as markers. A zero at row 1, column 1 is recorded by writing 0 at row 1, column 0 and at row 0, column 1.

blocks.text: Two details that make it work

**Why a separate flag for column 0?** The corner cell `matrix[0][0]` would have to mean two things at once — "row 0 has a zero" and "column 0 has a zero". One cell can't hold both, so column 0 gets its own boolean, `firstColHasZero`, and the marking loops start at `c = 1`.

**Why the second pass runs backwards?** The markers live in row 0 and column 0. Applying them top-to-bottom would overwrite row 0's markers before the rows below had read them. Working from the **bottom-right** corner means every marker is read before it is overwritten.
Dry run it yourself
Watch the markers appear in the first row and column (they're highlighted), then the second pass apply them row by row from the bottom.

Complexity

blocks.alt: Sets: O(m×n) time and O(m+n) space. Markers inside the matrix: O(m×n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.text: Two passes over the matrix: **O(m × n) time**, and a single boolean of extra memory: **O(1) space**.
Edge cases to test

items: **A zero in the first row** — `[[0, 1], [1, 1]]`: row 0 and column 0 must both clear.
**A zero in the first column only** — handled by `firstColHasZero`.

blocks.text: Where this idea shows up again

"Store your bookkeeping inside the input" is how many O(1)-space tricks work: marking visited numbers by making them negative in **Find the duplicate number**, or the index-as-address idea in the **Cyclic sort** chapter. Whenever the output doesn't need part of the input any more, that part is free memory.
